newsitem.title: JAPAN: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - JAPAN OIL SPILL.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - JAPAN OIL SPILL.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Fears of a repeat of the 1989 Exxon Valdez Alaska oil pollution disaster swept through Japan this week after news that Tokyo Bay was threatened by a 13,400 tonnes oil slick, spewing from the ruptured tanker Diamond Grace.
Government sources initially believed the spill to be the worst in Japan's history which threatened environmental damage on an unprecedented scale.
That it was Japan's second major spill in six months horrified insurers facing the prospect of massive claims for the clean-up and led to the inevitable cries of "something must be done".
The relief that Diamond Grace has turned out to be about one tenth the size of initial estimates was surpassed only by the embarrassment of government officials who overplayed the scale.

Instead of shedding 13,400 tonnes of crude into Tokyo Bay, a more modest 1,315 tonnes is now thought have been lost, making it a substantially smaller spill than the 5,200 tonnes dumped in Niigata Bay in January by the Russian tanker Nakhodka, the second worst oil disaster on record in Japan.

The financial costs of the latest spill will consequently fall well below the US$194 million International Fund for Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage limit, saving the tanker owner and their insurers a hefty sum.
But the accident has again raised the stakes in the debate about safety practices and tanker construction.

Age of vessel has long been an underwriter's primary concern when assessing risk weightings, a point which irks owners of increasingly aged fleets who say construction and maintenance standards are more vital.

The rupturing of the nearly new Diamond Grace, commissioned before the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) July 1993 ruling that all new tankers be built with double hulls, adds weight to the argument that youth is not the ultimate test.

Going against is the fact that the vessel was a single hull tanker, adding to the concern that the shipping industry is still some way from achieving safety standards that many marine underwriters would be more comfortable with.
It could easily be 20 years before the IMO's 1993 rules become the de facto standard for all tankers at sea.
Short of demanding retro-fitting on all single hull tankers, insurers will have to live with the risks.
But while hull rates are at historic lows, the power of insurers to make such demands is puny.
